transcript: Breaking news for people who are the same kind of nerd as me. We finally have a trailer for the new Hamlet adaptation starring Oscar-winner Riz Ahmed. Here are my takeaways They are mostly positive, but I have one big concern. So for context, this version has a modern setting, but more specifically, it's told through the lens of a family of South Asian heritage. The trailer shows us bits of Morfydd Clark as Ophelia and Timothy Spall as Polonius. And of course, the big star, Academy Award winner Riz Ahmed in the title role. On the positive side, this is a fantastic cast, and I love the angle, the concept. I feel like it's gonna bring exciting perspective. The trailer has kind of an exhilarating, almost thriller-like energy to it, which I think could work very well. We get to see bits of “to be or not to be” performed behind the wheel of a moving car, which seems like a great take. Also a little Easter egg. It might be too dark to see it here, but there's some graffiti that says “Frick Elsinore” But the most interesting thing I noticed from the trailer is that it seems to be a bit of a hybrid with some of Shakespeare's original dialogue mixed in with new lines of dialogue that are designed to kind of sound like Shakespeare. Now, to be very clear, I'm not a purist by any means. I think there's plenty of ways to mess around with Shakespeare and make it even feel more accessible that work very well. And I don't object to any of it on principle. But writing entirely new dialogue that's meant to sound like Shakespeare, but isn't? it's just extremely difficult to do well. Like, for example, I think two of the most embarrassingly botched, absolute train wreck film adaptations of Shakespeare were 2019’s “The King starring Timothee Chalamet, and the 2013 Romeo and Juliet starring Hailee Steinfeld. And they both use this approach. And even a little bit worse in Romeo and Juliet, because as it was more of a hybrid. Cause putting imitation Shakespeare next to real Shakespeare is just a very dangerous game. I tend to think it's genuinely better to just go all the way in the other direction and write entirely contemporary dialogue. But interestingly, one of the lines that I think is a completely new line that's in the trailer. At least I can't find it in the full text, or the 1st or 2nd quarto is where Gertrude says, “we grieved your sickly father while he lived” which is actually in iambic pentameter and does sound more or less like Shakespeare. So if they can pull it off, you know, power to them. I'm definitely gonna go in with an open mind and hoping to love it.
